comments.author: Aiswarya Venkitesh
comments.comment:
Most AI roadmaps put evals after agents, but that order is backwards. If you can't measure retrieval quality, tool-call success, and failure modes, agents become guesswork. Which stage is your current bottleneck: chunking, reranking, or state management?

#AIEngineering #RAG #Evals

comments.author: Jonny Tooze
comments.comment:
LLM judges are useful, but they should never be the sole blocker. In production agentic systems, I gate deploys on deterministic schema and tool use checks, then use the judge for soft signals and route disagreements to humans. How are you measuring judge-human agreement when the rubric changes?

#Evals #AgenticAI

comments.author: Jasson Franklyn
comments.comment: I keep seeing the same failure mode: not agent capability, but unscoped tools. A narrow agent with read-only access, rollback, and eval gates beats a generalist with broad write access every time. Which guardrail has saved you the most pain in production? #AgenticAI #Evals #LLM

comments.author: Shivani Virdi
comments.comment: The hidden tax in MCP is context: every tool description is sent with every request, so 30+ tools can make the model pick wrong more often. I’d treat dynamic tool search and sandboxed code execution as core architecture, not optional. How do you test whether a model actually chooses the right tool at scale? #MCP #AgenticAI #LLMOps

comments.author: Gabriel Laranja
comments.comment: Agents are cheap; the factory is the expensive part. I treat each agentic PR as a bounded task with entry criteria, output checks, and a kill switch. What is your hardest gate when a bot asks for repo write access? #AgenticAI
